title: Competition for eggs or sperm suffices to define sexual selection: a comment on Janicke (2024)
content: There is an easy way to define sexual selection: it occurs when there is competition among individuals for resources provided by mates. But there are practical challenges in deciding if a resource is limited, thereby forcing individuals to compete. For example, on a lek, there are many males, and there is seemingly no need for females to compete for sperm. Even so, in some lekking species, females still fight over males (Hare and Simmons 2019). These fights raise a question: when do certain males offer resources that should be excluded from the pool of resources available to females, thereby turning an apparent surplus into scarcity? There is something troubling about a definition that requires limited resources but can only identify them based on observations of competition. This challenge is even more troubling when we accept that competition is often subtle. Kokko (2021) provides an example of male copepods that benefit by swimming faster than their rivals, whom they might never directly encounter, because these males have a higher encounter rate with sexually receptive females. Females are implicitly rare enough that one male's mating success comes at another male's expense. This challenge, not mentioned by Janicke (2024), echoes past debates about how to calculate the operational sex ratio: should it be restricted to those “qualified” to mate (Ahnesjö et al. 2001)?
